Kirkstall
KURK-stawl
n. (the Cistercian abbey founded from Fountains in 1152, now a ruin in a public park in the middle of Leeds)
From Old Norse kirkja, a church, with Old English stall, a place or site; the church site.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kirkstall Abbey was founded in 1152 when Henry de Lacy gave the Aire valley site to a colony from Fountains, and it was built quickly and almost entirely in one campaign, which is why it is the most coherent Cistercian plan left in England; most of the church walls and the chapter house stand. It grew wool and ran iron forges, declined after the Black Death, and was dissolved in 1539. Leeds then grew out to meet it: the abbey now sits in a public park between a main road and the river, in the middle of a manufacturing city, with a museum in its gatehouse. The dictionary records Kirkstall for that setting, which is a parable nobody arranged. A house built in an empty valley to be away from the world ended with the world built around it, and Christ's metaphors for his people are not withdrawal but salt and light, both of which only work in contact: salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing, and a light is set up in order to be seen and to make God glorified.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines salt as a substance used to season and preserve; savour as taste and flavour; to shine as to emit light; to glorify as to honour; and darkness as absence of light.

expand to see more

SALT, n. Common salt, used to season food and to preserve meats from putrefaction; taste; smack; savor.

SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste and smell; flavor.

SHINE, v.i. To emit rays of light; to give light; to be bright; to be lively and animated.

GLORIFY, v.t. To praise; to magnify and honor in worship; to make glorious; to exalt to glory.

DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; obscurity; a state of being intellectually clouded; wickedness.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:13 — "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men."

Mat 5:16 — "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."

Isa 9:2 — "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined."

2Co 4:6 — "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ."

Modern Corruption

Cistercian abbey founded from Fountains in 1152 in an empty Aire valley, now a ruin in a public park in the middle of Leeds.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ's figures for his people both require contact with what they act upon. Salt is useless once it is only itself: “if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing” (Mat 5:13). Light exists to be looked at and to redirect attention: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16).

The live temptation is the one the Cistercians institutionalised, a holiness measured by distance, and the irony of Kirkstall is that a city came and settled around the retreat. Isaiah's promise is about light arriving where people already are: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa 9:2). And Paul locates the illumination inside believers, for the purpose of being carried out of them: God “hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2Co 4:6). A park full of people round a ruined church is not a defeat.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek halas (G0217), salt; Greek moraino (G3471), to make tasteless; Greek lampo (G2989), to shine; Hebrew owr (H0216), light.

expand to see more

Greek halas (G0217) — salt; “Ye are the salt of the earth”, Matthew 5:13.

Greek moraino (G3471) — to make foolish or insipid; “if the salt have lost his savour”, Matthew 5:13.

Greek lampo (G2989) — to shine, to give light; “Let your light so shine before men”, Matthew 5:16.

Hebrew owr (H0216) — light; “have seen a great light”, Isaiah 9:2.

Greek photismos (G5462) — illumination; “to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God”, 2 Corinthians 4:6.

Usage

"“it is thenceforth good for nothing” (Mat 5:13) — salt kept apart from food."

"“Let your light so shine before men” (Mat 5:16) — light exists to be seen."

"“hath shined in our hearts” (2Co 4:6) — in order to be carried out."
